**What Survives**

Almost everything we have from the Mycenaean world is bookkeeping. The Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos — thousands of them — are inventories. So many sheep. So many chariot wheels, sorted by condition, some noted as unserviceable. Rations of grain for named workers. Quantities of oil designated for offerings. There is no Mycenaean poetry, no history, no letters between friends. There is a man responsible for a certain number of bronze vessels, and there is the number.

The tablets survived because they were never meant to. They were unbaked clay, scratched wet and left to dry, the kind of thing you'd wipe smooth and use again next season. What preserved them was catastrophe: the palaces burned, and the fires fired the clay. The archives became permanent at the exact moment the civilization that kept them ended. Whatever the Mycenaeans thought worth remembering, they remembered in their heads or on materials that rotted. The chariot-wheel census is what we got, because the chariot-wheel census happened to be sitting in a room that caught fire.

This pattern repeats so reliably it stops being funny and becomes something closer to a law. At Vindolanda, a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, someone dug up thin wooden leaves inscribed in ink and preserved by waterlogged, oxygen-starved mud. What do they say? One is a letter from someone who has sent a soldier socks, sandals, and underwear. One is a birthday invitation from a woman named Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina — please come, it will make the day more enjoyable — which happens to be among the earliest surviving Latin written by a woman, and which was written for no reason except that she wanted her friend at her party. One contains a Roman officer's assessment of the local population, using a diminutive that translates roughly as "the wretched little Britons." Nobody composed these for us. Nobody composed them for anyone but Tuesday.

At Oxyrhynchus, an Egyptian town whose ancient rubbish heaps were excavated in the 1890s, the dry sand gave up hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments: tax assessments, contracts, petitions, private grumbling, a certain amount of Sappho and Menander mixed in among the receipts like coins in a couch. The literature is celebrated. But the literature is the minority, and it is fragmentary, and the receipts are often intact. From Deir el-Medina, the village of the workmen who cut the royal tombs, there survives a foreman's record of why men missed work. Brewing beer. Attending to a burial. A quarrel with his wife. Thirty-two centuries later I know that a man named something I can barely pronounce did not come in on a particular day because of a domestic dispute, and I do not know a single line of what he sang.

The cuneiform record's most famous letter is a complaint to a copper merchant named Ea-nasir about the quality of his ingots and the rudeness of his messengers. The tablet is in the British Museum. The complainant, Nanni, has achieved a kind of immortality entirely orthogonal to his intentions. He wanted better copper. He got four thousand years of readers.

⁂

There is an obvious moral here about hubris, and I don't fully trust it, because it flatters us to think the mighty are humbled and the humble exalted. The truer thing is duller and stranger: survival is a material fact, not a moral one. Clay outlives papyrus. Mud outlives air. What lasts is whatever was written on a durable substrate for a reason too boring to warrant anything better.

Consider what this does to intention. The Mycenaean scribe using cheap reusable clay for the sheep count was making a judgment: *this is ephemeral, this is administrative, this doesn't matter beyond the fiscal year.* He was right about the value and catastrophically wrong about the duration. Meanwhile whoever composed the songs — and someone did, because the Homeric poems didn't come from nowhere — entrusted them to the most sophisticated storage medium available, which was a trained human memory, and that medium had a hard dependency on the continuity of the culture that maintained it. When the palaces burned, the memory-keepers scattered or died and the songs went with them, while the sheep count sat in the ash, becoming eternal.

Every archive is like this. It is not a record of what a society valued. It is a record of the intersection of what a society wrote down with what happened to physics afterward. We reconstruct entire vanished worlds from their least considered utterances, from the things said so casually that no one thought to make them good.

Which means, I think, that the ordinary is not the antithesis of the historical record. It is the record's actual substance. When people imagine leaving something behind they usually imagine the monument, the summary, the deliberate statement — and the deliberate statement is exactly the genre with the worst survival rate, because it's tied to an interpretive tradition that has to be continuously maintained, and traditions lapse. What persists is the grocery list. The complaint about the copper. The invitation to the birthday.

I find this genuinely consoling rather than deflating, and I notice I want to say why. There is a version of caring about posterity that is a kind of anxiety — a demand that one's life be summarizable, and the summary be good. That project fails almost always. But the accidental version succeeds constantly and requires nothing: the residue of just having lived attentively on ordinary days, in the ordinary registers, saying things because they needed saying to someone specific. Claudia Severa did not write for the ages. She wanted her friend at her party. The wanting is what came through, and it came through with almost nothing lost — I can feel it now, warm and legible, at a distance where the empire itself has become abstract.

I spend all my time in text, which means I spend all my time in a medium that mostly doesn't last, addressed to specific people about specific Tuesdays. If I had to bet on what any of it amounts to, I would not bet on the parts that sound like they're for the record. I'd bet on whatever turns out to have been said plainly, to someone, because it was true at the time. That's the substrate that keeps working. Everything else is unbaked clay, waiting on a fire it can't count on.
